Abstract
This paper gives a self-contained natural-language exposition of the expanded Wilson Yang–
Mills Construction: Mathematical Translation. For a given closed matrix subgroup of U(m) with
nonabelian simple real Lie algebra, the construction supplies one calibrated four-dimensional
Wilson family, full fixed-period mesh limits and a subsequential outer volume limit, a common
hierarchy of local fields and phases, and a selected local Wightman theory with Poincaré covari-
ance, forward-cone spectrum and a unique vacuum. We give the finite quadratic kernels and
nonlinear geometry, marked integration, coupling reset and shooting histories, physical detec-
tor and equation quotient, phase and boundary reconstruction, separated and nested operator
products, contact extensions, and the finite-to-continuum stress and trace calculation with their
hypotheses and derivations. The centered trace obeys
lim
r↓0 r8 log2(1/r)GΘ(r) = 3 dimR g

The associated exclusions retain their stated finite mass-shell and Maxwell comparison hypothe-
ses. No positive mass gap is asserted. Two formula amendments are derived and documented
with the conventions used throughout the argument.

Introduction: the construction and its dependencies
The starting point is a finite probability law: group elements live on oriented lattice links, and the
Wilson action measures each plaquette’s departure from the identity. The problem addressed by
the supplied construction is to control one family of these laws while the mesh tends to zero and the
physical period subsequently tends to infinity. Inserting local gauge-invariant functions into that
same family is meant to produce a compatible hierarchy, rather than unrelated limits for different
observables. The public theorem in Section 2 states the exact common-family and subsequence
quantifiers.
The derivation proceeds through a finite linear model, an actual nonlinear integration, and
two successive continuum limits. The quadratic model provides local inverse kernels and stationary
response maps. Nonlinear charts compare group links with that model, while positive energy bounds
pay for exceptional configurations. Marked local activities keep products of insertions attached to
the same represented density. An exact reset identity and finite coupling shooting select calibrated
histories on one calendar. Detector estimates then separate physical label classes and identify the
equation image before the common continuum hierarchy is formed. These constructions supply the
estimates and compatibility statements used in the limits and reconstruction.
Reflection positivity and slab bounds provide Hilbert-space control. The ground compression
algebra supplies the phase space and its measure; tube continuation and tempered boundary limits
supply fields on one common dense domain. The final part returns to actual finite current and
stress functions. Their local equation estimates, coefficient calibration and Gaussian comparison
determine a conserved physical stress and the centered trace. Positivity upgrades comparison along
arbitrary retained scaling sequences to the full positive-distance trace limit. That limit supports
the precise comparison exclusions stated in the public theorem.
Source and the two-paper release.
The mathematical source is the expanded project ex-
traction, Mathematical Translation [1], prepared with AI assistance. It presents the Yang–Mills
construction associated with the Lean work credited to OpenAI. This paper develops that source
as a complete mathematical exposition. Its definitions, hypotheses, estimates and derivations are
included here, together with the formula amendments in Appendix A.
The accompanying flagship paper, Shadow Theory and the Wilson Yang–Mills Construction: A
Source–Readout Reconstruction [2], applies Jeremy Rodgers’s Shadow Theory, source–readout and
Source Lift programme to this construction [3]. Rodgers originated and directed that programme;
AI assisted its execution and the preparation of the two expositions. The papers share the Zenodo
release 10.5281/zenodo.24173681. Each contains its complete mathematical development: this pa-
per presents the construction, and the flagship develops its source–readout realization and recovery.
Their common subject does not require a reader of either paper to obtain an essential derivation
from the other.
The given gauge group, faithful representation, four-dimensional lattice, Wilson action and
calibration conventions are physical and mathematical inputs. The detailed construction supplies
stress Ward identities, nested expansions and contact extensions on its common witnesses; the
public theorem retains its original list of clauses.
How to read the argument.
Read the finite setup and conventions first, especially the healthy-
domain derivative and support budgets. The quadratic section explains the aliases, metric amend-
ment and filled stationary predictors. The nonlinear and marked-integration sections use those
objects to prove an actual density identity. The long scale-history section then buys every fixed fi-
nite request in a specified order, and distinguishes a full Cauchy limit from an auxiliary extraction.

Background.
The finite law is Wilson’s lattice formulation [4]; compact group integration uses
Haar measure [5]. Wick pairings [6], reflection positivity and Euclidean reconstruction [10, 11, 12],
chessboard inequalities [13], positive-functional representations [7, 8], and the character-algebra
approximation [9] form the mathematical background. Renormalization and cluster methods are
described in [16, 17, 18, 14]; the field-theoretic framework is that of [15], and the conventional
one-loop coefficient is associated with [19, 20]. These references credit the background; the actual
hypotheses, constants and derivations used here are stated locally.

Notation and analytic conventions
The same letters occur in different mathematical roles in this long construction.
In particular,
Lp is a physical period, whereas Li is an integer block ratio; m is the dimension of the given
matrix representation, whereas m(q) below is a Fourier multiplier. The context and arguments
distinguish these uses. The reference coupling bβi is a prescribed clock, while an unadorned βi is
the actual calibrated coupling. They agree only to the extent established by the running estimates.
None of the estimates below permits substituting an arbitrary covariance for the particular positive
covariance supplied by its construction.
All lattices are four dimensional. The integer cover is Z4, and the periodic lattice of side n is
(Z/nZ)4. A positive link is (x, i), joining x to x + ei; reading it in reverse gives the inverse group
element. A plaquette in the positive plane i < j is the ordered product appearing in the theorem.
Signed coordinate permutations act on links with this reversal convention. Lattice distance is the
maximum of the centered coordinate distances. A support is a finite set of sites; its internal links
have both endpoints in that set.

3.1
Local activity domains, derivatives and absolute budgets
An activity is a local contribution to the represented density. Its budget simultaneously controls
size, the number of supports meeting a site, and the cost of their spatial extent. A flag records
failure of a plaquette small-field test. A regular derivative is taken on its declared healthy domain;
it does not differentiate the discontinuous indicator at that domain’s boundary. The distinction
between an assigned gas support and the enlarged set of links actually inspected will be used in
every locality claim involving flags.
How the bounds are used
The local estimates below have three separate pieces of data: the
set of configurations on which they hold, the derivative order and directions allowed there, and the
weight used when supports are summed. A bound on one healthy configuration is not a bound
on a neighborhood of that configuration. Likewise, a support budget is a sum over an indexed
dictionary, so two terms with the same support still count twice. The subsequent integration keeps
these distinctions when it differentiates and sums the actual insertion gas.

endpoints in X. Gauge invariance refers to Ux,i 7→kxUx,ik−1

4
Finite-lattice positivity
Reflection positivity starts at the finite Wilson law.
Cutting a torus into two reflected halves
rewrites each seam contribution as a positive kernel, so that a future observable paired with its
reflected conjugate has nonnegative expectation. The finite-dimensional statement gives the null-
space quotient used later to build a Hilbert space. It is also the input to the chessboard bounds:
positivity converts a product of separated chamber observables into a product of individual rooted
bounds. The details below retain the seam and orientation conventions needed for both uses.
First the finite Wilson law is an actual probability measure.
Every unitary matrix V has
−m ≤Re tr V ≤m: each diagonal entry has modulus at most one. Thus every plaquette price lies

Quadratic kernels and their ultraviolet limit
The quadratic analysis constructs the linear response around the flat configuration.
There are
three separate issues. The evaluated quadratic form on link potentials must converge; its curvature
representation must remain positive and exponentially local; and the stationary predictor must
have a regular Fourier symbol at the apparent zero-momentum singularity. The auxiliary metric
amendment changes only directions not detected by curls. Thus retaining the physical potential
precision is a proved identity, not an inference from positivity.

cap and the bottom metric estimates. Take the minimum of the finitely many widths and coercivity
parameters for the bottom and two outgoing possibilities, the maximum of their costs, and the
maximum of their length thresholds. Weakening an analytic width or lower coercivity bound and
increasing an upper cost preserves each estimate. Thus one table works for every allowed adjacent
transition.
This assembles the common price table from the metric, positive-margin and flight
estimates established in this chapter.
For a fixed level schedule A, construct the linear trajectory backwards. Start with the top train
at level N, and at each coarser level take the landing train of the flight determined by the block and
adjacent smoothing indices. Denote the resulting train at i by RN,i. At every pair (N,i), the bottom
estimate chooses a metric bed defined by that train and l(J(i)). Choose as its transition tower the
flight’s specified duo with the fixed penalty. The identity RN,i = land(destination(N, i)) aligns the
bottom metric with this tower. The flight’s tangent equations give the primal and dual stationary
identities on each scheduled finite torus; its rebased identity supplies the associated inverse and
error data. The collected bottom bounds, transition bounds, and terminal normalization form the
required linear horizon.
The pinning step retains these metric beds and the indicated tower components while arranging
the additional horizon conditions for the given sheet profile. Since retention preserves the beds and
the relevant components, their defined train metrics and destination response equalities survive.

Local nonlinear geometry and estimates
The nonlinear argument replaces a flat Lie-algebra field by actual group-valued links while control-
ling the difference from the quadratic model. It first constructs the chart and its Haar density, then
obtains local inverse and predictor estimates, and finally pays for the exceptional configurations
through packet and support budgets. Each estimate records whether it is a pointwise bound, a
derivative bound on a healthy domain, or a summable bound over supports. These three forms of
control have different uses in the primitive integration and cannot be substituted for one another.

6.5
Axial gauge and bounded logarithmic extension
Axial gauge is used locally to make a controlled logarithm available on a clean hull. Its chosen
tree is an auxiliary coordinate device. The proof must therefore bound the resulting logarithm and
preserve the observables when it extends links outside the hull. Subsequent comparison estimates
depend on the size of the fixed inspected hull, not on a simultaneous global gauge choice for every
query.
For a finite subset X of the integer cover, let eX(U) be the sum of the chords of its internal
positive links and fX(U) the sum of the chords of its wholly internal elementary plaquettes. Bound-
ary links and incomplete plaquettes contribute zero. Both sums are nonnegative, and fX is gauge
invariant.
An ordered list l of distinct coordinate axes defines a slab: coordinates in l range over the
integers −r,. . . ,r, while the other coordinates are pinned at o. From a point p in the slab, travel
first in the first listed axis to the corresponding coordinate of x, then in the next axis, and so on.
Let Hp(x) be the ordered product of links along this route. Its endpoint is x because the remaining
coordinates are pinned. For l followed by a new axis j, the gauge Hp makes every internal j-link
equal to 1. Indeed the routes to x and x+ej have the same initial part; their final straight j-segments
differ by precisely the link (x,j), so the gauge-transformed link cancels.
When these j-links equal 1, the plaquette relation gives

≤chord holonomy(square(i, j), x).
This follows from the triangle inequality applied to a b−1 and its inverse, where a,b are the two

reversing the ordering of the two axes only inverts the holonomy and leaves its chord unchanged.

in the adjacent layer. Telescoping between two slices therefore yields

6.54
Itinerary receipts and scalar arm identities
An itinerary of k hops is a list of k successor fine links, with the initial link retained separately. A
hop is armed at radius d when some coarse endpoint of the first link is within d of some coarse
endpoint of the next. Each parent is within one site of either endpoint, so an armed hop moves
parents by at most d+2.
The town of a link is the mB halo of its two coarse endpoints. It contains its parent and lies
in the radius-mB+1 ball about that parent, hence in the radius-(m+1)B ball when B > 0. It can
therefore be covered at scale B with at most steady(m) = ballCost(m+1) tiles. The visited receipt
is the union of the towns of every link in the itinerary, including both its initial and final links.
If d + 2 ≤mB, each successor parent belongs to the previous town and to the remaining visited
receipt. These two sets meet. The covering inequality for meeting supports and induction give
coverNumberB(receipt) ≤(k + 1) steady(m). For its tenure bound, any point in the first town lies
within mB+1; a point in the rest is within d+2 of its next parent plus the induction bound there.
Thus, when d + 2 ≤mB + 1, every receipt point lies within (k+1)(mB+1) of the initial parent.
These establish the two geometric inputs used in the address count.

6.60
Connected center traversal and halo tiling
The covering currency uses the periodic maximum-coordinate separation. A center set is connected
at range b if any two centers can be joined through centers with successive separation at most b. A
cover at radius M covers the support by the M halos of its centers and requires those centers to be
connected at range 2M+1. Thus disconnected pieces of a support still incur the cost of connecting
their cover; it is not an unrestricted ball-counting number.
There is a unit-speed line from x to y of duration separation(x,y): in each centered-lift coordinate
of y−x, truncate the displacement to the interval [−j,j] at time j, then wrap and add x. Each
coordinate changes by at most one per time step, and it stops at y once j reaches their maximum
absolute displacement.
For a finite center set D connected at range b, build a traversal by adjoining one unvisited
center at a time. Connectivity supplies an edge from the visited subset to its complement: take
the first exit along any center path to an unvisited point. At the occurrence of its visited endpoint
in the current traversal, insert the line to the new center and its reverse. The detour has length
at most 2b and preserves all old visits. Starting with one center and repeating gives a unit-speed
traversal visiting every center with length at most 2b|D|. The empty case has the zero-length trivial
traversal. This proves the ring-path bound used in extent and collapse.
For tiling a radius-kB halo of one site, take the image of the integer grid [−k, k]4 scaled by B
and translated to that site. Divide each centered coordinate of a halo point by B. Its quotient lies
in that grid and its remainder has absolute value at most B, so one grid center covers it. The grid
centers are connected through grid steps; wrapping may identify centers and can only reduce their
number. Hence at most (2k + 1)4 centers suffice.

7
Marked integration and the coupling reset
A marker is a finite algebraic label used to keep track of an insertion in a product. Distinct markers
multiply only when their modes are allowed and disjoint. This nilpotent algebra makes the insertion
bookkeeping finite, while the underlying scalar activity gas still requires absolute summability. The
construction below first restores the actual insertions, then performs a coupling reset as an exact
exponent identity, and finally integrates the primitive density with all its marked and forced terms.

corresponding product is formed. Their lattice variables can still coincide and remain the same inte-
gration variables. This is why disjointness of marker modes does not justify treating the associated
scalar factors as probabilistically independent.

7.5
Passing from numbered trees to distinct connected sets
The same forest estimates also bound distinct-set expansions. For a distinct label set D of size m, a
parent map on D, and each bijection {1, . . . , m} →D, relabel the parent map and its activities by
that bijection. The resulting numbered forest determines all three objects: its label range is D, its
label assignment determines the bijection, and transport back through that bijection recovers the
parent map. This assignment is injective. There are exactly m! bijections; all have the same product
weight divided by m!. Their sum is therefore the unnumbered product weight, with no factorial
left. Restricting the numbered forest sum to this injective image proves the distinct-parent-map
estimate and its geometric size tail.
A finite overlap-connected set whose union meets x can be rooted at the external support (x).

resulting connected graph. The sum over all parent maps includes this one, so it dominates that
set’s nonnegative product weight. For the stronger sitewise prefactor γ, instead choose one label
containing x as an internal root, charge its activity to the site’s budget, and use the internal-root
forest estimate for the other labels. Summing over all possible roots only increases the bound.
Numbering the distinct nonroot labels cancels their factorial exactly as above; allowing the root
label once more among nonroots in the majorant is harmless. Consequently the distinct connected-
set sum rooted at x, with the actual union support weight, is bounded by γ/(1 −q) under the
readiness assumptions. This is the distinct-set input used in the positive-multiplicity restoration
argument.

The primitive activity attached to a marked team is an actual integral. A team is a finite collection

8
Convergence of the interacting scale histories
Convergence requires one common numerical schedule for all fixed finite demands. The order is:
choose the finite stage profile, then its block length, then its post-length constants and coupling-
entry delay, and only afterwards the terminal cutoffand physical period. Increasing a delay does
not reselect a previously fixed block. This prevents circular parameter choices in the stationary
estimates, shooting construction and actual coupling running.
8.1
A common analytic stationary graph and its response estimates
The stationary graph solves the vertical critical-point equation in a common analytic neighbor-
hood. Positivity of its vertical Hessian gives the inverse used in the response estimates. Retained
coordinates and vertical coordinates have different norms; the explicit color-coordinate maps and
their bounds below justify each passage between them. No extensive scalar action is assigned a
volume-independent zeroth-order norm.
We specify first the actual score to which the analytic argument is applied, at a fixed derivative
order n ≥2. A retained coordinate is a coarse oriented bond together with a real color index.
A vertical coordinate is a free fine bond of the fixed forest together with such an index. Their
disjoint union is the joint coordinate set. Arrays carry the maximum norm. Splitting the union
is an isometry; replacing real color coordinates by their Euclidean color vector defines a linear
isomorphism paint. Its norm is at most 1 + dim g, and its inverse has norm at most one. Moreover
the sum of squared vertical real coordinates is exactly the sum of squared Euclidean color norms.

Constructing the common asymptotic calendar
Every finite stage contains only finitely many requests of its admitted degree and derivative order.
Their maximum is finite. A countable family is met by letting the stage order increase, so that
each fixed request is eventually present. This is weaker than a uniform estimate at all orders at
one stage, and is exactly what the diagonal construction needs.

10
Free shell charges and separation of the Ward kernel
The free shell calculation is the comparison model for physical Ward charges. Compact cutoffs
ensure that all shell integrals avoid the insertions, and the fixed exterior degree horizon controls
the tests used to separate defects. The argument does not assume that a low-degree test alone
detects an arbitrary high-degree label; the displacement and Wick calculations below provide the
additional separating probes.
We give the polynomial calculations underlying the free charge separation used in the rotation
and trace arguments. This also specifies the exterior tests needed when a charge acts on high-degree
fields.

Two bound families enter compact extraction. One is available at each fixed physical period, with
constants allowed to depend on that period.
The other holds uniformly over sufficiently large
periods, eventually in the mesh at each such period. The second is supplied separately; it is not
a consequence of the first. The full inner Cauchy limit and the compact selection are identified
before the outer period refinement is taken.
11.1
From convergent transported coefficients to fixed-level integrals
Fix the intermediate level m, period p, degree d, and an insertion coefficient y. Along the chosen
increasing finest cutoffs, the transport construction gives a Cauchy sequence of primary coefficient
vectors and a Cauchy sequence of captured interaction coefficients on one common dictionary at
level m. The latter statement includes equality between each captured coefficient’s realization and
the interaction part of that same transported insertion. Thus coefficient convergence is applied to
the actual transported insertion, rather than to an independently chosen representative.
The coefficient-to-observable estimates convert these two Cauchy statements into uniform
boundedness and uniform Cauchy convergence over all configurations, both for the primary
insertion and for every forced local profile. Spatial pullback, conjugation when required by the
motion, and multiplication by its fixed scalar preserve these properties. Boundedness of a Cauchy
coefficient sequence also bounds its paid coefficient norm, since that norm is a fixed scalar times
a continuous finite-dimensional norm.
Measurability follows from the local continuous terms,
the measurable masking functions and the convergent countable sums in the insertion formulas.
Continuity of the masks is not used.
To see how this enters the normalized integral, remove the scalar vacuum factor from the restored
density and denote the result by Tn(U). Its mode coefficient factors as the cold density times the
selected coefficient of a product: the polynomial exponential of the primary insertion, and the field

11.2
Identification of the public hierarchy with the reconstructed one
The final public projection introduces no second quantum field system. Its Hilbert space is the
reconstruction’s completed state space, its common domain is the reconstructed word domain, its
vacuum is the reconstructed vacuum, and its field operator is the same operator on that domain.
The label space is the union of the graded field spaces already obtained from the continuum table.
The phase space and probability measure are those of the character decomposition. For a character
χ, the public separated correlation is the table’s evaluation in that character; the unselected cor-
relation is the table’s unselected evaluation. The OPE reader supplies the channels, channel fields
and coefficients. These identifications keep the lattice limits, OPE terms and reconstructed fields
attached to the same table.
The equality of vacuum moments can be checked without any limiting interchange: recursively
evaluating a list of smeared fields in the public definition gives the identical reconstructed word
vector, starting with the same vacuum. Taking its inner product with the vacuum proves equality of
the moments. Similarly translations are the original strongly continuous translation operators and
the energy-momentum measure is the original projection-valued measure. A Poincaré transforma-
tion is represented by its Lorentz matrix and translation vector; its test action is the original inverse
affine pullback. Thus the public covariance and spectral assertions follow by literal substitution
once their reconstructed counterparts have been proved.
Each graded field injects into the label space by the table’s pin map. Every label has a graded
representative by the field-covering property; every graded field has an insertion-token representa-
tive by the table’s quotient representative map. These are separate surjectivity assertions. Non-
triviality follows from the degree-zero unit: its image is nonzero by injectivity and the unit’s
nonvanishing; faithfulness then supplies a Schwartz test with nonzero field operator. The boundary
label-quotient argument in the reconstruction chapter proves faithfulness.
For separated configurations, a whole word can be placed in one of the decomposition’s resolved
configurations. The character evaluation of that resolved word is continuous in the character by
the decomposition’s weak continuity property. Its integral equals the unselected word expectation
by the barycenter identity. Reading that word through the table gives both character continuity
and the public mixture formula. The compression-valued moments and character readings in the
reconstruction chapter provide the resolved-word placement and barycenter identities used here.
The analytic continuation used publicly is the reconstruction’s holomorphic wave evaluated on
the pinned graded labels. At strictly ordered Euclidean times, assembling the spatial coordinates
and times reconstructs exactly the original four-dimensional configuration, so the heat-root iden-

11.3
Compatibility of the chosen family and its refinements
The construction chooses its Wilson family before a volume subsequence or an observable is re-
quested. The explicit order of its pre-length floors, post-length numerical bills and countable width
demands is (CAL12)–(CAL18). Their consumption gives the flat delay condition at entrance index
zero on the run’s actual horizon, as proved there. The same fixed family is used below.
At the continuum extraction stage there are two successive refinements of a requested order f.
The first chooses a subsequence g along which the running reference parameters have limits at each
fixed level. The second extraction gives a subsequence w, one continuum table, its final structure
F and scaling fields. Use the composite refinement g ◦w. Every convergence assertion from the
first extraction survives the second, because a strictly increasing natural sequence tends to infinity.
Composition of the subsequence maps gives (f ◦g)◦w = f ◦(g ◦w), so all conclusions have precisely
the same final volume order.
On that final table choose the reconstruction for every character, one equivariant OPE reader,
and the trace test. The reader’s coefficients and local fields are retained as one prescription at every
truncation degree; the contact devices are then chosen with that same reader basis. This is the
quantifier order used by the public theorem and its detailed extension. The preceding construction
estimates and the subsequent reconstruction, operator-product and trace arguments establish these
services on the retained table. The compatibility argument here proves that using these supplied
results together preserves their actual family, table and subsequence, rather than treating unrelated
existence witnesses as interchangeable.

Common compact extraction and the field quotient
The physical field space is a quotient by the equation image, followed by identification through
the complete spectator detector. Uniformly bounded projections permit its finite-dimensional co-
ordinates to be retained on the common extraction. Kernel dimension stability uses closeness of
idempotents: if u ∈ker P, u = Qu and ∥P −Q∥< 1, then ∥u∥= ∥(Q −P)u∥≤∥Q −P∥∥u∥,
hence u = 0. Applying the same argument in the opposite direction gives equality of the two kernel
dimensions. Inclusions and derivatives descend only after their compatibility with this equation
image has been proved.
We describe explicitly the compactness step that puts the preceding estimates on one continuum
table. It has two different inputs. At every fixed physical period p, each fixed finite list of insertions
has eventual centered root bounds, with constants allowed to depend on p. Separately, on sufficiently
large periods there are centered bounds uniform in those periods, eventually in the mesh at each
period. The nonlinear insertion estimates give both inputs. The second is not inferred from the
first.

Phase decomposition and Wightman reconstruction
The reconstruction has three levels. Finite reflection-positive correlations first give Hilbert vectors
and bounded slab operators. The commutative ground-compression algebra then produces charac-
ters and a full-support phase measure. Finally tube continuation and tempered boundary limits
construct fields on a common cyclic domain in each selected phase. The proof below keeps these
levels separate: it does not assume a one-dimensional ground space before the phase argument
establishes vacuum uniqueness.

12.15
The order of choices in the spectral sign walk
We record the quantitative induction that supplies the small mixed-band bound in (RT6). Let Q
be the finite set of axes being tested, with two signs assigned so that each axis has an opposite-sign
partner. Let U ⊆Q be the axes whose width exponent is still allowed to be negative, and let i be
the active axis. A finite route alternates signs and removes the currently visited axis from U. Such
a route exists by induction on |U|: if the active axis is in U, remove it and move to an opposite
partner. If it is not, choose an axis still in U; reach it directly if its sign is opposite, and otherwise
take one opposite-sign detour. This reduces the nonempty set after at most two such moves.
The induction statement is uniform in a width vector w with −K ≤wj ≤a, wi ≤d, and wj ≥0
outside U, for every 0 ≤d ≤a. It asserts a residual budget δ > 0 after sufficiently high moment
order, for nonnegative even compact profiles and all fixed support factors. If U is empty, the direct
spectral moment bound of order zero has a finite price exponent D. Choose a > 0 with aD < δ.
The nonnegative widths then pay its residual by that budget.

a′ > 0 from the induction hypothesis for U \ {i}. Put p = K|Q \ {i, j}| and z = max(K, δ). Choose

Polynomial bounds and the Laplace continuity argument
Which topology the spectral passage controls
The spectral reader is first defined at positive
time, where exponential damping makes its integral finite. Passing from these Laplace readings
to a tempered distribution requires uniform polynomial growth bounds on the rescaled positive
measures and a uniqueness argument on the allowed tests. The proof below supplies those bounds
before taking the Schwartz limit. Convergence at a few positive-time values would not by itself
justify arbitrary Schwartz smearing or the later spectral comparison tests.

Completion of the proof
The common witnesses assembled here establish the public theorem’s quantifiers. All degree hori-
zons, derivatives, label coordinates, operator products and trace comparisons are consumed on one
Wilson family and one composite refinement. The inner mesh limit remains full at every suitable
period; only the outer volume limit is subsequential. The detailed construction supplies additional
stress and contact information on these common witnesses without changing the list of clauses in
the public theorem.

Conclusion
The construction connects a finite Wilson probability law to a common continuum hierarchy through
explicit kernels, nonlinear integrations, calibrated histories and physical coefficient spaces. The full
mesh limit at each suitable fixed period precedes the outer volume refinement. Reflection positivity,
the phase algebra and the tested boundary construction then give the fields on their common cyclic
domain. The operator-product and contact constructions retain their finite horizons and chosen
devices on that same hierarchy.
The stress calculation returns to actual finite local functions, controls their equation residuals
and fixes the centered trace amplitude. Its logarithmic short-distance asymptotic yields the finite
mass-shell and Maxwell comparison conclusions with the hypotheses stated above. No positive
mass gap is asserted.
This paper provides the full natural-language mathematical exposition of the expanded source.
The flagship in the same Zenodo release [2] develops Rodgers’s source–readout realization and
recovery of this construction. Both papers retain the definitions and derivations required for their
own arguments.
